learningObjectives: Explain why receptor subtype determines effect.
Summarise major roles of glutamate, GABA, dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline and acetylcholine.
Avoid simplistic one-transmitter explanations of psychological disorders.

anatomy.label: Glutamate
anatomy.detail: Glutamate activates AMPA, NMDA and metabotropic receptors across cortical and subcortical circuits.
anatomy.clinical: Excessive glutamatergic activation can contribute to excitotoxicity, while NMDA-dependent signalling supports plasticity.

anatomy.label: GABA
anatomy.detail: GABA-A receptors usually increase chloride conductance; GABA-B receptors act through slower G-protein mechanisms.
anatomy.clinical: Reduced inhibitory control can increase network instability and seizure susceptibility.

anatomy.label: Dopamine
anatomy.detail: Dopamine modulates prediction error, motivation, movement and working-memory gating through several receptor families and pathways.
anatomy.clinical: Effects differ markedly across nigrostriatal, mesolimbic, mesocortical and tuberoinfundibular pathways.

anatomy.label: Serotonin
anatomy.detail: Serotonin acts through many receptor subtypes to influence mood, sleep, appetite, pain and behavioural adaptation.
anatomy.clinical: SSRIs change transporter function quickly, but therapeutic adaptation usually unfolds over weeks.

anatomy.label: Noradrenaline
anatomy.detail: Locus-coeruleus projections modulate vigilance, signal-to-noise ratio and responses to uncertainty.
anatomy.clinical: Both insufficient and excessive arousal can impair executive performance.

anatomy.label: Acetylcholine
anatomy.detail: Basal forebrain acetylcholine supports attention and cortical plasticity; other cholinergic systems regulate motor and autonomic function.
anatomy.clinical: Cholinergic loss is prominent in Alzheimer disease, while anticholinergic burden can impair cognition.

interaction.title: Neurotransmitters sequence
interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to see how the system changes over time.

stages.label: Synthesise
stages.text: Enzymes produce transmitter or load it into vesicles.

stages.label: Interpret
stages.text: Receptor subtype and circuit location determine the effect.

stages.label: Adapt
stages.text: Reuptake, metabolism and receptor regulation shape future signalling.

quizBank.question: Why can the same neurotransmitter have different effects?
options: Different receptor subtypes and circuits interpret it differently
Its molecules change colour in each brain region
quizBank.explanation: Receptor coupling and circuit context determine functional effect.

quizBank.question: Which pair dominates fast cortical excitation and inhibition?
quizBank.explanation: Glutamate and GABA are the principal fast excitatory and inhibitory transmitters.

quizBank.question: Dopamine is best understood as:
options: A context-dependent modulator of learning, salience and action
The single chemical cause of pleasure
A hormone that never acts in brain
quizBank.explanation: Dopamine has pathway- and receptor-specific roles beyond pleasure.

quizBank.question: Why do SSRI clinical effects usually lag behind transporter blockade?
options: Downstream network and receptor adaptations take time
Serotonin must physically grow new neurons first
The blood–brain barrier opens only after weeks
quizBank.explanation: Immediate transporter effects lead to slower adaptive changes across systems.

quizBank.question: High anticholinergic burden may particularly impair:
quizBank.explanation: Acetylcholine supports attention and memory, especially in basal forebrain systems.
